\chapter{All the Way Up, and On a Sign}
\label{ch:ka-ordinals-to-tenth}
\hlchaptermodality{75}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say sixth to eleventh in Kannada, use the everyday short ending, and read an ordinal written as a digit.}

Read an ordinal written as a Kannada digit with only its ending spelled out, and say the whole word aloud.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[āraneya]{\kn{ಆರನೆಯ} (āraneya) — sixth}

\label{lesson:KA-C75-sixth}



\begin{quote}
The line goes on past five, so the chapter opens by retrieving where it stopped.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{aidaneya} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eraḍaneya}, and say what you did to \emph{eraḍu} to build it — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{innondu}, and say what the \emph{innu-} adds — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gāḷi} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಆರನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಆರನೆಯ}} (\emph{āraneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sixth}\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\kn{ಆರು}} drops its \textbf{-\kn{ು}} and takes \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}}, with nothing else to notice.

\textbf{\kn{ಆರನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{āraneya dina}), the sixth day.

That \textquotedblleft{}nothing else to notice\textquotedblright{} is the point of the whole chapter. Six to ten were a separate lesson from one to five when you learned to count; for ordering they are not a separate anything.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āru}, then \emph{āraneya}
  \item \emph{aidaneya, āraneya}
  \item \emph{āraneya mara} — the sixth tree
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the sixth day\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\kn{ಆರನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}}.) Did the ending change above five? (\textbf{No}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ēḷaneya]{\kn{ಏಳನೆಯ} (ēḷaneya) — seventh}

\label{lesson:KA-C75-seventh}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{āraneya} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mūraneya} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{innondu sala hēḷi} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mañju} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಏಳನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಏಳನೆಯ}} (\emph{ēḷaneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{seventh}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\kn{ಏಳು}} has the retroflex \textbf{\kn{ಳ}}, the letter Kannada shares with Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam and which northern languages lost. Adding the ending does not soften it: \textbf{\kn{ಏಳನೆಯ}}, with the tongue still curled back for the \textbf{ḷ}.

\textbf{\kn{ಏಳನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{ēḷaneya dina}), the seventh day.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ēḷu}, then \emph{ēḷaneya} — keep the ḷ retroflex both times
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āraneya, ēḷaneya}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಏಳನೆಯ} and find the \kn{ಳ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the seventh day\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\kn{ಏಳನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}}.) What happens to the \kn{ಳ} when the ending goes on? (\textbf{Nothing}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eṇṭaneya]{\kn{ಎಂಟನೆಯ} (eṇṭaneya) — eighth}

\label{lesson:KA-C75-eighth}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ēḷaneya} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{modalaneya}, and say what word it is built on — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yāvāga} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{maraḷu} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಎಂಟನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಎಂಟನೆಯ}} (\emph{eṇṭaneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{eighth}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\kn{ಎಂಟು}} carries the \textbf{\kn{ಂ}} anusvara, the dot that takes its sound from whatever follows it — here a retroflex \textbf{ṇ}, because \textbf{\kn{ಟ}} is retroflex. The ending is added at the far end of the word, so the dot keeps the same neighbour and the same sound.

\textbf{\kn{ಎಂಟನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{eṇṭaneya dina}), the eighth day.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{eṇṭu}, then \emph{eṇṭaneya}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ēḷaneya, eṇṭaneya}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಎಂಟನೆಯ} and find the \kn{ಂ} still sitting before \kn{ಟ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the eighth day\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\kn{ಎಂಟನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}}.) Why does the \kn{ಂ} still sound like ṇ? (Because \textbf{\kn{ಟ}} is still the letter after it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ombattaneya]{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತನೆಯ} (ombattaneya) — ninth}

\label{lesson:KA-C75-ninth}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eṇṭaneya} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nālkaneya} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\kn{ವ}}, and say its sound — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kesaru} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತನೆಯ}} (\emph{ombattaneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ninth}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು}} is the longest cardinal in the set: an anusvara, a doubled \textbf{\kn{ತ್ತ}}, and four syllables. None of that matters to the ending, which does what it did to the two-syllable \textbf{\kn{ಆರು}} — takes the final \textbf{-\kn{ು}} off and goes on after everything else.

\textbf{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{ombattaneya dina}), the ninth day.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ombattu}, then \emph{ombattaneya}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{eṇṭaneya, ombattaneya}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತನೆಯ} and find the doubled \kn{ತ್ತ} untouched
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the ninth day\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}}.) Did the length of the cardinal change what the ending does? (\textbf{No}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hattaneya]{\kn{ಹತ್ತನೆಯ} (hattaneya) — tenth}

\label{lesson:KA-C75-tenth}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ombattaneya} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{aidaneya} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yāva}, and say how it differs from \emph{yāru} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{beṅki} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಹತ್ತನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಹತ್ತನೆಯ}} (\emph{hattaneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tenth}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\kn{ಹತ್ತು}} is the word that showed you the \textbf{p $\to$ h} law: Tamil kept \emph{pattu}, Kannada softened the p to h. The ordinal keeps whatever the cardinal became — the ending has no opinion about the history of the word it lands on.

\textbf{\kn{ಹತ್ತನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{hattaneya dina}), the tenth day.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hattu}, then \emph{hattaneya}
  \item \emph{ombattaneya, hattaneya}
  \item all ten in order, from \emph{modalaneya}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the tenth day\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\kn{ಹತ್ತನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}}.) Which sound law made \emph{pattu} into \emph{hattu}? (\textbf{p $\to$ h}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hannondaneya]{\kn{ಹನ್ನೊಂದನೆಯ} (hannondaneya) — eleventh, and the edge that is not there}

\label{lesson:KA-C75-eleventh}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hattaneya} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{āraneya} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bandāga}, and say what its ending means — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hasu} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಹನ್ನೊಂದನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಹನ್ನೊಂದನೆಯ}} (\emph{hannondaneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{eleventh}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\kn{ಹನ್ನೊಂದು}} was itself a built word: the ten-echo \emph{hann-} with \emph{ondu} welded on. Now the ordinal ending goes on top of that, and the result is a word made of three parts, none of which had to be learned as a whole.

\textbf{\kn{ಹನ್ನೊಂದನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{hannondaneya dina}), the eleventh day.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending is a fact about numbers, not about ten}]
Most books stop an ordinal chapter at \emph{tenth}, and a learner reasonably concludes that the ten words were the set. In Kannada there is no set. \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}} attaches to a number, and every number you learn from here on arrives with its ordinal already made: \textbf{\kn{ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು}} gives \textbf{\kn{ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತನೆಯ}} (\emph{ippattaneya}), twentieth, without a lesson.

That is why this book taught the ending in the second lesson of the previous chapter rather than after ten examples. The examples were never the content.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hannondu}, then \emph{hannondaneya}
  \item \emph{hattaneya, hannondaneya}
  \item take \emph{ippattu} and make its ordinal yourself
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the eleventh day\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\kn{ಹನ್ನೊಂದನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}}.) Do you need a lesson for \emph{twentieth}? (\textbf{No} — the ending goes on any number.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[modalanē]{\kn{ಮೊದಲನೇ} (modalanē) — the short form you will actually hear}

\label{lesson:KA-C75-short-form}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hannondaneya}, and say why \emph{ippattaneya} needs no lesson — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ēḷaneya} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nanage cahā bēku} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mēke} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮೊದಲನೇ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲನೇ}} (\emph{modalanē}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{first}\textquotedblright{}, again.

In speech the ending \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}} is usually shortened to \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೇ}}. The \textbf{\kn{ಯ}} goes, the \textbf{\kn{ೆ}} lengthens to \textbf{\kn{ೇ}}, and that is all:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{careful} & \textbf{everyday} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ}} \emph{modalaneya} & \textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲನೇ}} \emph{modalanē} \\
\textbf{\kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ}} \emph{eraḍaneya} & \textbf{\kn{ಎರಡನೇ}} \emph{eraḍanē} \\
\textbf{\kn{ಮೂರನೆಯ}} \emph{mūraneya} & \textbf{\kn{ಮೂರನೇ}} \emph{mūranē} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both are worth having, and for different reasons: you need to recognise the long one on a printed page, and you need to produce the short one at a door.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{modalaneya}, then \emph{modalanē}
  \item \emph{eraḍanē, mūranē}
  \item \emph{modalanē dāri} — the first road
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the everyday short form of \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}}? (\textbf{-\kn{ಅನೇ}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}the third road\textquotedblright{} the way a neighbour would. (\textbf{\kn{ಮೂರನೇ} \kn{ದಾರಿ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\kn{೧ನೇ} — the ordinal on a street sign}

\label{lesson:KA-C75-on-a-sign}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{modalanē} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eṇṭaneya} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\kn{ಜ}}, and say its sound — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kōḷi} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the digit does the counting for you}]
Written Kannada rarely spells an ordinal out. It writes the \textbf{digit} and hangs only the ending on it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{written} & \textbf{read aloud} & \textbf{means} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{೧ನೇ}} & \emph{modalanē} & 1st \\
\textbf{\kn{೩ನೇ}} & \emph{mūranē} & 3rd \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You already read \textbf{\kn{೧}} and \textbf{\kn{೩}}; those were script lessons back in chapters 9 and 11. What is new is only that \textbf{\kn{ನೇ}} may follow a digit, and — this is the part that catches a reader out — that you say the \textbf{whole} word aloud even though only its tail is written. \textbf{\kn{೧ನೇ}} is not read \textquotedblleft{}one-nē\textquotedblright{}. It is read \emph{modalanē}, a word with no \kn{ಒಂದು} in it, off a sign that shows the digit for one.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The Kannada digits were taught one at a time across chapters 9 to 18 and, until now, there was nothing in this book to read them in. This is what they were for: a street sign, a floor number, a bus route and a date are all written this way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\kn{೧ನೇ}} and say it aloud in full
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\kn{೩ನೇ}} and say it aloud in full
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\kn{೧ನೇ} \kn{ದಾರಿ}} — the first road, as a sign would write it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\kn{೧ನೇ}} aloud. (\emph{Modalanē} — not \textquotedblleft{}one-nē\textquotedblright{}.) What is written on the sign, the whole word or its tail? (\textbf{Its tail}, after the digit.)
\end{tcolorbox}
